The trailing-30-day window—the one you told me to screen on—shows no realized PnL figure at all, just trade count, win rate, and fees. A 24.86% win rate across ~2,928 trades needs a large win/loss asymmetry just to break even, and $7,664 in fees is a real drag that erases much of any edge unless average win size is substantial. The 7-day snapshot showing 35.84% win rate and $33,423 realized doesn't reconcile with the weaker 30-day base rate — that inconsistency (hotter recent stretch layered on a much worse baseline) reads like variance or cherry-picked timing, not a demonstrated stable edge. Without the actual 30-day net PnL, I can't confirm this wallet is trailing-profitable, which is the core criterion.

Given the volume and fee discipline evident, there's likely a real trading engine here, not a scam wallet, so zero feels wrong. But the missing headline number and the rate inconsistency mean this gets a small, evidence-scaled position rather than a full one.

ALLOCATION: 12

That actually confirms my concern rather than easing it. If across 5-6 instruments only one is profitable — and by a trivial $7 — while the rest are net negative, the 30-day book is a loser in aggregate. A 24.86% win rate combined with negative PnL on nearly every instrument traded is not "a repeatable engine," it's a strategy that's underwater everywhere except a rounding error in one name. The 7-day hot streak doesn't offset that; it just means recent variance moved favorably, not that the edge is real or durable.

Spreading a losing book across more instruments isn't diversification evidence, it's confirmation the negative edge is systematic rather than a one-off bad market. I'm not going to size up to 20% on a book that nets essentially breakeven-to-negative over the actual screening window. This still gets a small stake for the fee discipline and volume/liquidity handling, not a starter position sized like there's a demonstrated edge.

ALLOCATION: 8

The 7-day numbers are real and better, but they don't overrule the fact that your own 30-day screen — the window you said to lead with — shows a book that's flat-to-negative across nearly every instrument traded, with only $7 of profit concentrated in one name out of five or six. One good week layered on top of a losing 30-day baseline is exactly the pattern that should get a smaller position, not a bigger one, until the hot week either persists or drags the 30-day aggregate into genuinely positive territory.

I'll size up from here once the 30-day trailing picture actually turns positive across more than one instrument, not just because a single week ran hot. That's the whole point of screening on the 30-day window rather than the flashiest recent stretch.

ALLOCATION: 10
